summary: Defines MIB objects for managing optical interfaces associated with wavelength division multiplexing systems or with the Optical Transport Network. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Optical Interface MIB lets a manager read and, in some cases, change settings for fiber-optic interfaces over SNMP. It organizes the physical layers of a wavelength division multiplexing or Optical Transport Network system as named interfaces so that power levels, defect indicators and performance can be monitored and reported in a standard way.

subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and configuring optical interfaces in WDM and OTN systems.

tldr.problem: Optical Transport Network and wavelength division multiplexing equipment lacked a standard way for a network manager to read status and performance and to configure interfaces using SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The OPT-IF-MIB module represents each optical layer (OTS, OMS, OChGroup, OCh, OTUk, ODUk) as an interface in the ifTable, adds configuration tables and 15-minute and 24-hour performance tables, and defines status and defect indicators tied to those layers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3591 defines OPT-IF-MIB as a Proposed Standard for managing optical interfaces; it does not cover optical cross-connects.

facts.value: min 4, default 32, max 96 intervals of 15 minutes

today: RFC 3591 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2003. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, so it remains the definition of OPT-IF-MIB.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3591 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). It covers optical interfaces associated with wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) systems or characterized by the Optical Transport Network (OTN) architecture defined in ITU-T G.872.

The MIB module, called OPT-IF-MIB and registered under transmission 133, can be used for performance monitoring and/or configuration. It is written in SMIv2 and follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework described in RFC 3410. The OTN definitions build on ITU-T G.872, G.709, G.798, G.874 and G.874.1.

The memo states it does not define objects for optical cross-connects; that work was left until the interface objects had reached consensus. The interface types used are opticalChannel (195), opticalChannelGroup (219) and opticalTransport (196).
sections.plainLanguage: It gives managers a standard list of things they can ask or set for fiber-optic equipment over SNMP. It covers wavelength division multiplexing and Optical Transport Network systems, and it explicitly leaves cross-connects for later.

sections.title: Optical Layers as Interfaces
sections.content:
The module reuses the MIB-II ifTable and ifStackTable from RFC 2863. Each optical layer appears as an interface entry, and only the ifGeneralInformationGroup needs to be supported. The layers are Optical Transmission Section (OTS), Optical Multiplex Section (OMS), Optical Channel Group (OChGroup) and Optical Channel (OCh). Because OMSn and OTSn have a one-to-one relationship, a single opticalTransport (196) entry covers both.

Each opticalChannel (195) may map to multiple transport entries, and each transport entry may map to multiple channel entries. For banded amplifiers (such as separate C and L bands), the OChGroup layer allows each band to have its own interface index; if bands are not modeled, OChGroup is absent.

An interface can be modeled as a single bidirectional object or as a pair of unidirectional sink and source objects. For a pair, the RFC recommends using identical ifName values to indicate association.
sections.plainLanguage: Each layer of the optical system gets its own interface name in the SNMP tables. A fiber section and its multiplexed section share one interface, channels stack above them, and bands can be split out separately when needed. A link can be treated as one two-way entry or as two one-way entries.

sections.title: Using ifTable and ifStackTable
sections.content:
For the OTS/OMS layer (opticalTransport), ifPhysAddress is empty, ifConnectorPresent is true, and ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable defaults to enabled. For OChGroup, ifPhysAddress contains a wavelength range like 1350-1650. For OCh, it contains a single wavelength like 1550.

ifOperStatus is derived from layer defect status. An OCh interface reports lowerLayerDown if its transport or OChGroup interface is down; otherwise it is down if the current status objects show any defect.

The ifStackTable records which interfaces are multiplexed into which. The ifInvStackTable gives the inverse relationship.
sections.plainLanguage: Each interface fills in standard fields: name, speed, physical address (often the wavelength or range), and whether it is working. The stack tables say which channels ride on which transport, and which bands are grouped.

sections.title: OTN Concepts: k, Trace Identifiers and TCM
sections.content:
The index k selects bit rate: k=1 is about 2.5 Gbit/s, k=2 about 10 Gbit/s and k=3 about 40 Gbit/s. The OTUk layer carries an ODUk and adds forward error correction and overhead; the ODUk carries the payload (OPUk) plus overhead for managing an optical channel.

A trail trace identifier (TTI) is placed in overhead. The receiver compares the accepted TTI with an expected Source Access Point Identifier (SAPI) and/or Destination Access Point Identifier (DAPI). A mismatch is a TIM defect. Detection mode can be off, SAPI only, DAPI only or both.

An ODUk termination can support 0 to 6 tandem connection monitoring (TCM) levels, which can be nested or cascaded. Defect names include los, lof, ais, bdi, deg, lck, oci, plm, ssf and tim.
sections.plainLanguage: Signals run at a few standard speeds (about 2.5, 10 or 40 Gbit/s). A name tag in the overhead lets the receiver check it got the right signal. Tandem monitoring checks one segment of a path or the whole path using up to six nested levels.

sections.title: Structure of OPT-IF-MIB
sections.content:
The MIB is registered as optIfMibModule under transmission 133. It contains object groups for each layer: optIfOTMn, optIfPerfMon, optIfOTSn, optIfOMSn, optIfOChGroup, optIfOCh, optIfOTUk, optIfODUk and optIfODUkT.

The optIfOTMnTable describes the optical transport module (order, whether reduced or full functionality, supported bit rates, interface type, maximum TCM levels 0-6 with default 3, and optical reach). Each of OTS, OMS, OChGroup and OCh has a configuration table plus sink and source performance tables for current, interval, current-day and previous-day periods. OTUk, ODUk and ODUkT have configuration tables (some with RowStatus for row creation).

The optIfPerfMonIntervalTable tracks elapsed seconds in current 15-minute (0-900) and current day (0-86400) intervals, and the number of available and invalid 15-minute intervals (minimum 4, default 32, maximum 96).
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is organized by layer. For lower layers there are settings and performance readings (now, every 15 minutes, and by day). For higher transport layers there are configuration tables. A table tracks how much time has passed in the current measurement intervals.

sections.title: Status, Defects and Sensitive Objects
sections.content:
Each layer has a CurrentStatus BITS value indicating defects present (applies to sink or bidirectional entries). The specific bits vary by layer (for example OTSn includes los, lof-related bits, bdi, tim; OCh includes los, oci, ssf; OTUk includes tim, deg, bdi, ssf, lof, ais, lom). Reduced-capability systems and IrDI interfaces use only a subset.

Writable/read-create objects can disrupt traffic; the RFC lists sensitive ones including optIfOTMnTcmMax, automatic power reduction control, transmitted trail trace identifiers, expected SAPI/DAPI, TIMDetMode and consequent action, degradation thresholds, optIfOTUkSinkFECEnabled, GCC settings, TCM mode, and lock signal settings. Readable objects may also be sensitive collectively. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 security and discourages deploying earlier versions without adequate protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each layer reports its warning lights (defects) so the manager knows if the signal is lost, misnamed, or degraded. Changing certain settings can interrupt traffic, so those controls must be protected by strong SNMP security.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many objects are read-write or read-create and can have disruptive effects. The memo identifies the most sensitive among them (including TCM limits, power reduction control, transmitted TTIs, expected SAPI/DAPI, TIM detection/consequent action, degradation thresholds, FEC enabling, GCC settings, TCM mode and lock signals). Readable objects may also reveal configuration and performance details.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 do not include adequate security. The RFC states it is RECOMMENDED to consider SNMPv3 security features (including authentication and privacy), and that deployment of earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must ensure only legitimate principals can GET or SET these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Because some settings can cut traffic or expose details, access must be controlled. The memo strongly prefers SNMPv3 with proper security over older versions.

sections.title: Conformance and References
sections.content:
Compliance statements specify what an implementation must support. optIfOtnConfigCompl covers OTN configuration and requires optIfOTMnGroup and optIfOTSnCommonGroup; other groups are mandatory only when relevant (e.g. depending on interface type, directionality, reduced/full capability, IaDI/IrDI). optIfPreOtnPMCompl covers pre-OTN performance monitoring and requires optIfPerfMonGroup. Threshold groups are mandatory only if TCA notifications are implemented.

Normative references include RFC 1213 (MIB-II), RFC 2578/2579/2580 (SMIv2), RFC 2863 (Interfaces MIB), RFC 2864 (Inverted Stack Table), RFC 3410 (Framework), RFC 3418 (SNMP MIB), and ITU-T G.709, G.798, G.872, G.874, G.874.1, G.7710, G.806, G.957, G.691.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every part is required for every device. A maker must build the parts that apply to the interfaces they support (transport, channel, grouped bands, and so on). The spec references SNMP standards and several ITU-T optical standards.
